Die Quotienten-Regelmiene der.

MATH 11.41.title: Wasslu als rata
MATH 11.41.context: A bakery reports its total weekly cost $C(Q)$ in euros when it bakes $Q$ loaves, and it also reports the average cost per loaf $A(Q)=\dfrac{C(Q)}{Q}$. Management wants the approximate extra cost of baking one more loaf near the current output. Decide WAHR or FALSCH for each claim.
MATH 11.41.solution_overview:
The bakery reports total weekly cost $C(Q)$ and average cost per loaf
$$A(Q)=\dfrac{C(Q)}{Q}.$$
Management's question — the approximate extra cost of one more loaf — is answered by the derivative of total cost (marginal cost):
$$C^{\prime}(Q).$$
On a graph of $C$ against $Q$, that derivative is the slope of the tangent. The linear approximation near any named output reads
$$C(Q+\Delta Q)-C(Q)\approx C^{\prime}(Q)\,\Delta Q,$$
so with $\Delta Q=1$ and $C^{\prime}(120)=0.80$ one gets about $0.80$ euros of extra cost. In general $A(Q)$ and $C^{\prime}(Q)$ are different functions; they meet only at special points such as an average-cost minimum.

MATH 11.46.title: Grenznutzen in einfacher Sprache
MATH 11.46.context: Die Zufriedenheit eines Verbrauchers aus $x$ Freizeit wird durch eine Versorgungsfunktion $U(x)$ gemessen. Entscheiden Sie für jede Behauptung die Wahrheit oder die Lüge.
MATH 11.46.solution_overview:
Satisfaction from $x$ hours of leisure is measured by a utility function $U(x)$. Marginal utility is the derivative
$$U^{\prime}(x),$$
not the stock $U(x)$ itself. The linear approximation
$$U(x+\Delta x)-U(x)\approx U^{\prime}(x)\,\Delta x$$
shows that the sign of $U^{\prime}$ answers the local question: if $U^{\prime}(x)>0$ a little extra leisure raises satisfaction, while if $U^{\prime}(x)<0$ a little extra leisure lowers it. MATH 11.62.title: Z. Z. Z. Z. Z.
MATH 11.62.context: A small workshop can run its regular crew for up to $50$ units a week. Up to that point every unit costs a steady $12$ euros of labour and materials, so weekly cost is $C(Q)=12Q$ whenever $0\le Q\le 50$. Beyond $50$ units the crew must be paid overtime: the workshop still pays the $600$ euros already spent on the first $50$ units, and then $20$ euros for each extra unit, which is written $C(Q)=600+20(Q-50)$ when $Q>50$. Customers are willing to pay enough that marginal revenue stays at $R'(Q)=16$ euros per unit for every $Q>0$. Judge every assertion below.
MATH 11.62.solution_overview:
Regular-crew cost is $C(Q)=12Q$ for $Q\le 50$, so
$$C^{\prime}(Q)=12\qquad(Q<50).$$
Beyond capacity, $C(Q)=600+20(Q-50)$ gives
$$C^{\prime}(Q)=20\qquad(Q>50).$$
Crossing into overtime therefore raises the cost of an extra unit by $20-12=8$ euros. Marginal revenue is constant at $R^{\prime}(Q)=16$. Comparing slopes:
$$P^{\prime}(40)=16-12=4>0,$$

MATH 11.184.title: Klinikdurchsatz: f, f' und f in der
MATH 11.184.context: A clinic tracks a throughput index $f$ (brown), its Ableitung $f^{\prime}$ (green) und its second Ableitung $f^{\prime\prime}$ (purple) on one shared figure. Throughput is measured against a staffing intensity $x$. Welche der folgenden Aussagen ist/sind korrekt?
MATH 11.184.solution_overview:
The figure stacks three related curves against staffing intensity $x$: brown is the throughput level $f$, green is its slope $f^{\prime}$, and purple is $f^{\prime\prime}$.

Local extrema of brown sit where green crosses the axis and changes sign: near $x=1$ green flips $-$ to $+$, so brown has a local minimum; near $x=5$ green flips $+$ to $-$, so brown has a local maximum.

An inflection of brown is a zero of purple with a sign change. Purple crosses through zero near $x=3$ (from $+$ to $-$), so $f$ changes from concave up to concave down there.

By definition $f^{\prime\prime}=(f^{\prime})^{\prime}$, so wherever purple is negative (right of $x=3$), green must be decreasing. The peak of green is only the steepest climb of brown — not a turning point of brown — and at the inflection $x=3$ green is still positive, so throughput is still rising toward its maximum near $x=5$.
statements: Brown has a local minimum near $x=1$ and a local maximum near $x=5$.
Purple crosses zero near $x=3$, and that is an inflection of brown: concavity of $f$ changes there.
Where purple is negative (right of $x=3$), green is decreasing — matching $f^{\prime\prime}=(f^{\prime})^{\prime}$.
Der höchste Punkt von Grün ist ein lokales Maximum von Braun.
At $x=3$, brown is climbing, green is positive, and purple is near zero — so staffing intensity $3$ maximises throughput itself.

**A.** → Wahr

Brown is the throughput level $f$, and green is its slope $f^{\prime}$. Local extrema of brown therefore sit where green crosses the axis and changes sign — not where green merely peaks.

Near $x=1$, green passes from negative to positive, so the slope of throughput flips from downhill to uphill: brown bottoms out there — a local minimum.

Near $x=5$, green passes from positive to negative, so the climb of brown turns into a descent: brown peaks there — a local maximum.

Those two turning points are exactly the ones named in the claim.

$$
x = 1
$$

$$
x = 5
$$

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

Purple is $f^{\prime\prime}$, the concavity meter for brown. An inflection of $f$ is a zero of $f^{\prime\prime}$ where that second derivative changes sign — a flip of concavity, not a peak of the level itself.

The figure shows purple crossing through zero near $x=3$, switching from positive to negative. Left of that crossing brown is concave up; right of it brown is concave down.

So staffing intensity near $3$ is precisely an inflection of throughput $f$, which is what the claim asserts.

$$
x = 3
$$

By definition $f^{\prime\prime}=(f^{\prime})^{\prime}$, so the sign of purple is exactly the slope of green: purple positive means green is rising, purple negative means green is falling.

Wherever purple lies below the axis — which the figure shows for $x$ right of $3$ — green must be decreasing. That is not an extra geometric accident; it is the chain of derivatives written in colours.

The claim records exactly that consistency between the two derivative curves.

$$
f^{\prime\prime} = (f^{\prime})^{\prime}
$$

$$
x = 3
$$

which matches the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**D.** → Falsch

The highest point of green is where $f^{\prime}$ itself is largest — the steepest climb of brown — not a turning point of brown. At that staffing intensity, throughput is still rising as fast as it ever does.

A local maximum of brown requires green to cross through zero with a $+$ to $-$ sign change, which happens near $x=5$, well after green's peak.

The claim confuses a peak of the slope with a peak of the level.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

MATH 11.185.title: Keramikofen: Kostenbeugung und Grenzkosten
MATH 11.185.context: A ceramic kiln has weekly cost $C(Q)=Q^{3}-6Q^{2}+40Q+10$ for output $Q\ge0$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
MATH 11.185.solution_overview:
Weekly kiln cost is the cubic

$$C(Q)=Q^{3}-6Q^{2}+40Q+10\qquad(Q\ge 0)$$

Differentiate once for marginal cost and once more for concavity:

$$C^{\prime}(Q)=3Q^{2}-12Q+40$$

$$C^{\prime\prime}(Q)=6Q-12=0 \implies Q=2
$$

On $(0,2)$ one has $C^{\prime\prime}<0$, so $C$ is concave down and $C^{\prime}$ is decreasing; on $(2,\infty)$ one has $C^{\prime\prime}>0$, so $C$ is concave up. Thus $Q=2$ is an inflection of $C$ and the place where marginal cost stops falling.

Fixed cost is the level at zero output: $C(0)=10$. Equality $AC=MC$ is the different first-order condition for a critical point of $AC=C/Q$; it need not hold at the inflection $Q=2$.
statements: Marginal cost is $C^{\prime}(Q)=3Q^{2}-12Q+40$.
$C$ has an inflection point at $Q=2$.
On $(0,2)$, marginal cost is decreasing.
Durchschnitt verliert an jedem Wendepunkt an Grenzkosten von $C$.
At $Q=0$, fixed cost is $10$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Mit dem Ziel, das Ziel zu erreichen, ist es mit dem Ziel, okt ok"-bogen-S EIN - Kohäsions-Aspekt. $$
C(Q) = Q^{3}-6Q^{2}+40Q+10
$$ $$
C^{\prime}(Q) = 3Q^{2}-12Q+40
$$ Verwechseln Sie diese Ableitung nicht mit Durchschnittskosten $C(Q)/Q$; Grenzkosten sind die momentane Änderungsrate der Gesamtkosten, nicht der Durchschnitt pro Kopf.

Es besteht keine Notwendigkeit, weiter zu vereinfachen: Diese Quadratik ist bereits der beanspruchte Zeitplan. „22wandler,Ř2.........

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

An inflection of total cost is a zero of $C^{\prime\prime}$ where that second derivative changes sign. Differentiate the marginal-cost quadratic once more.

$$
C^{\prime\prime}(Q) = 6Q-12 = 0 \implies 6Q = 12 \implies Q = 2
$$

The trap would be stopping at $C^{\prime\prime}(2)=0$ without checking the sign change; here the flip from negative to positive confirms a genuine inflection.

On $(0,2)$ one has $C^{\prime\prime}<0$ (concave down), and on $(2,\infty)$ one has $C^{\prime\prime}>0$ (concave up). Concavity of $C$ therefore flips at $Q=2$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Wahr

Marginal cost falls precisely where its own derivative is negative — that is, where $C^{\prime\prime}<0$. From the second derivative already obtained,

$$
C^{\prime\prime}(Q) = 6Q-12 = 6(Q-2)
$$

Past $Q=2$ the second derivative turns positive, so marginal cost begins to rise — the interval $(0,2)$ is exactly the falling-MC region.

On the open interval $(0,2)$ one has $Q-2<0$, so $C^{\prime\prime}<0$ strictly. Therefore $C^{\prime}$ is decreasing throughout $(0,2)$, which is exactly the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**D.** → Falsch

An inflection of total cost is the condition $C^{\prime\prime}=0$ with a sign change. Equality of average and marginal cost is a different equation: it is the first-order condition for a critical point of $AC=\dfrac{C}{Q}$, coming from the quotient rule.

Those two algebraic conditions need not share the same root. At the inflection $Q=2$ there is no requirement that $AC=MC$ — confusing an inflection of $C$ with a critical point of $AC$ is the trap.

$$
C^{\prime\prime} = 0
$$

$$
AC = \dfrac{C}{Q}
$$

$$
Q = 2
$$

$$
AC = MC
$$

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**E.** → Wahr

Fixed cost is the cost of producing nothing — the value of the cost function at zero output, before any variable kiln runs.

$$
C(0) = 0-0+0+10
$$

$$
0 + 0 = 0
$$

$$
0 + 10 = 10
$$

$$
C(0) = 10
$$

Variable cost starts from zero at $Q=0$, so the entire $C(0)$ reading is fixed cost; nothing in the cubic's higher-degree terms contributes at the origin.

That matches the constant term in the cubic cost rule, and it is precisely the fixed-cost reading the claim asserts.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

MATH 11.186.title: Einfallsreicher: Einen für ein Wochenende
MATH 11.186.context: Ein Pop-up-Shop modelliert den Wochenendgewinn (Hunderte Euro) von $P(x)=x^{2}-6x+20$, wobei $x$ die Anzahl der besetzten Stunden ist. In einem der folgenden Aussprüche befindet sich:
MATH 11.186.solution_overview:
Weekend profit is the quadratic

$$P(x)=x^{2}-6x+20$$

The Newton quotient expands as

$$P(a+h)-P(a)=2ah+h^{2}-6h$$

$$\dfrac{P(a+h)-P(a)}{h}=2a+h-6$$

Sending $h\to 0$ (or differentiating directly) recovers

$$
P^{\prime}(x) = 2x-6 = 2(x-3)
$$

$$P^{\prime\prime}(x)=2>0$$

So $P^{\prime}<0$ on $(-\infty,3)$ and $P^{\prime}>0$ on $(3,\infty)$: $x=3$ is a local minimum, and profit is increasing for every $x>3$.

At $x=4$ one has $P^{\prime}(4)=2$ and $P(4)=12$, so the tangent is $y-12=2(x-4)$, hence $y=2x+4$, not the line $y=2x$.
statements: Der Newton-Quotient $\dfrac{P(a+h)-P(a)}{h}$ vereinfacht sich zu $2a+h-6$.
The tangent line at $x=4$ is $y=2x$.
Der Gewinn sinkt für alle $x>3$.
$x=3$ ist ein lokales Minimum von $P$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

The Newton quotient is the average slope of profit between $a$ and $a+h$. Expand the shifted value, cancel $P(a)$, and divide by $h$.

$$
P(a+h) = (a+h)^{2}-6(a+h)+20 = a^{2}+2ah+h^{2}-6a-6h+20
$$

$$
P(a+h)-P(a) = (a^{2}+2ah+h^{2}-6a-6h+20)-(a^{2}-6a+20) = 2ah+h^{2}-6h
$$

$$
\dfrac{P(a+h)-P(a)}{h} = 2a+h-6
$$

Sending $h\to 0$ in this quotient will recover $P^{\prime}(a)=2a-6$, but the claim only asks for the finite-$h$ simplification, which still carries the $+h$ term.

The simplified quotient is exactly $2a+h-6$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

Differentiate the quadratic profit rule, or send $h\to 0$ in the Newton quotient $2a+h-6$ (the $h$ term vanishes in the limit).

$$
P^{\prime}(x) = 2x-6
$$

$$
P^{\prime}(4) = 2\cdot 4-6 = 8-6 = 2
$$

The same value comes from the Newton quotient at $a=4$: $\lim_{h\to 0}(2\cdot 4+h-6)=2$, confirming the derivative calculation.

So the instantaneous rate of change of profit at four staffed hours is $2$ hundred euros per hour, matching the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Falsch

The tangent line at $x=4$ needs both the slope $P^{\prime}(4)=2$ and the point height $P(4)$ — slope alone does not determine the line.

$$
P(4) = 16-24+20
$$

$$
16 - 24 = -8
$$

$$
-8 + 20 = 12
$$

$$
P(4) = 12
$$

$$
y-12 = 2(x-4)
$$

$$
y = 2x-8+12 = 2x+4
$$

A line through the origin with slope $2$ would be $y=2x$, but the profit graph at $x=4$ sits at height $12$, so the tangent is shifted upward by $4$.

The claim writes $y=2x$, which keeps the correct slope but drops the intercept $+4$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**D.** → Falsch

Profit falls where $P^{\prime}<0$ and rises where $P^{\prime}>0$. Factor the derivative:

$$
P^{\prime}(x) = 2x-6 = 2(x-3)
$$

The critical point $x=3$ is a valley, not a peak: past three staffed hours each extra hour still raises weekend profit.

So $P^{\prime}<0$ on $(-\infty,3)$ and $P^{\prime}>0$ on $(3,\infty)$. For every $x>3$, profit is increasing, not decreasing — the claim reverses the sign chart past the critical point.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**E.** → Wahr

A local minimum occurs where $P^{\prime}$ changes from negative to positive, equivalently where $P^{\prime}=0$ and $P^{\prime\prime}>0$.

$$
P^{\prime}(x) = 2(x-3)
$$

$$
P^{\prime\prime}(x) = 2>0
$$

Because $P^{\prime\prime}$ is the positive constant $2$, the parabola opens upward, so the stationary point can only be a minimum.

At $x=3$ the first derivative flips $-$ to $+$, and the second derivative is positive, so $x=3$ is a local minimum of weekend profit.

$$
x = 3
$$

which matches the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

MATH 11.187.title: App Studio: Quadrat-Wurzel-Lernkosten
MATH 11.187.context: Die kumulativen Produktionskosten eines App-Studios für $Q>0$ Releases betragen $C(Q)=80\sqrt{Q}$. Welche der folgenden Aussagen ist/sind korrekt?
MATH 11.187.solution_overview:
Cumulative production cost is the square-root rule

$$
C(Q) = 80\sqrt{Q} = 80Q^{\frac{1}{2}}\qquad(Q>0)
$$

Power-rule differentiation and the average-cost quotient give

$$
C^{\prime}(Q) = MC(Q) = \dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}
$$

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{C(Q)}{Q} = \dfrac{80}{\sqrt{Q}}
$$

$$AC^{\prime}(Q)=-40Q^{-\frac{3}{2}}<0\qquad(Q>0)$$

so average cost falls throughout. Comparing the closed forms, $MC=\dfrac{1}{2}AC$ at every $Q>0$. Scaling output by two scales cost by $\sqrt{2}$ only: $C(2Q)=\sqrt{2}\,C(Q)$. At $Q=16$,

$$
C^{\prime}(16) = \dfrac{40}{4} = 10
$$
statements: Marginal cost is $C^{\prime}(Q)=\dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}$.
Average cost is decreasing for every $Q>0$.
Die Grenzkosten entsprechen der Hälfte der durchschnittlichen Kosten bei jedem $Q>0$.
Doubling cumulative output doubles total cost.
Bei $Q=16$ sind die Grenzkosten gleich $10$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Rewrite the square-root cost as a power and apply the power rule carefully.

$$
C(Q) = 80Q^{\frac{1}{2}}
$$

$$
C^{\prime}(Q) = 80\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}Q^{-\frac{1}{2}} = 40Q^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}
$$

As $Q$ grows, this marginal cost falls — each extra release costs less than the previous one — which is the learning-curve content of the square-root rule.

That is the claimed marginal-cost schedule: each extra release costs $40$ divided by the square root of cumulative output. Matching the expression to the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

Average cost is total cost per release. Divide, then differentiate with the power rule.

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{C(Q)}{Q} = \dfrac{80\sqrt{Q}}{Q} = \dfrac{80}{\sqrt{Q}} = 80Q^{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(Q) = 80\cdot\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)Q^{-\frac{3}{2}} = -40Q^{-\frac{3}{2}}
$$

A falling AC does not require falling total cost; here $C$ itself still rises because $MC>0$, while the average is pulled down by spreading the early expensive releases.

For every $Q>0$ this derivative is strictly negative, so average cost is decreasing throughout the positive domain.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Wahr

Compare the two closed forms side by side — both are constant over $\sqrt{Q}$.

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{80}{\sqrt{Q}}
$$

$$
MC(Q) = \dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}
$$

$$
\dfrac{MC}{AC} = \dfrac{40}{80} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

This half-relationship is special to the square-root (homogeneous of degree $1/2$) technology; it is not a general AC–MC identity.

So $MC=\dfrac{1}{2}AC$ at every $Q>0$, not just at a special output. That half-relationship is exactly the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**D.** → Falsch

Scaling cumulative output by $2$ scales a square-root cost by $\sqrt{2}$, not by $2$. The trap is treating $C$ as linear in $Q$.

$$
C(2Q) = 80\sqrt{2Q} = \sqrt{2}\cdot 80\sqrt{Q} = \sqrt{2}\,C(Q)
$$

Under linear cost, doubling output would double cost; under $C\propto\sqrt{Q}$ the scale factor is only the square root of two.

Total cost rises by the factor $\sqrt{2}\approx 1.41$, not by a factor of $2$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**E.** → Wahr

Evaluate the marginal-cost formula at the named output, taking the positive square root.

$$
C^{\prime}(16) = \dfrac{40}{\sqrt{16}} = \dfrac{40}{4} = 10
$$

Equivalently, $MC(16)=\tfrac12 AC(16)$ and $AC(16)=80/4=20$, so $MC=10$ again — the same numerical check.

Equivalently, $MC(16)=\tfrac12 AC(16)$ and $AC(16)=80/4=20$, so half of average cost is again $10$ — a second numerical check of the same formula.

So at sixteen releases the cost of one more release is $10$, matching the claim exactly.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

MATH 11.189.title: Kaffee-s au MU Unterbringungskosten dauernd
MATH 11.189.context: A coffee subscription models a subscriber's marginal utility of cups $c$ per month (brown). Each cup also has a constant opportunity cost of $6$ utility units, so the green curve is $\mathrm{MU}-6$. Interior cups are worthwhile while green is positive. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
MATH 11.189.solution_overview:
The figure plots a subscriber's marginal utility of cups $c$ (brown) together with the opportunity-cost gap

$$\mathrm{green}=\mathrm{MU}-6$$

a parallel downward shift of brown by the constant $6$. Interior cups remain worthwhile while green is positive.

Brown (MU) stays positive until it crosses the axis near $c=45$, so without the opportunity cost, utility of cups keeps rising until about that count. Green crosses zero near $c=30$, which is the stop rule $\mathrm{MU}=6$ and the best cup count among the plotted options.

At $c=10$, brown sits at height $14$, so green sits at $14-6=8$ (below height $10$). Because brown is linear and falling, $U^{\prime\prime}=(\mathrm{MU})^{\prime}<0$ throughout, so $U$ is strictly concave. Brown itself has no interior maximum on the window; the optimum is the zero of green, not a peak of brown.

Wenn man die Opportunitätskosten berücksichtigt, ist die beste Cup-Zahl der Abonnenten unter den aufführungsweisen Optionen in der Nähe von $c=30$, wo Grün Null kreuzt.
At $c=10$, green lies above height $10$.
Da Braun linear und fallend ist, ist die Nützlichkeit $U(c)$ in diesem Bereich streng konkav.
Is ins
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Without the opportunity cost, cups remain worthwhile while marginal utility itself stays positive — that is, while brown lies above the axis.

Brown crosses zero near $c=45$, so $\mathrm{MU}>0$ on $(0,45)$ and the subscriber's utility of cups keeps rising until about that count. Beyond $45$, brown is negative and additional cups would lower utility.

The claim records exactly that zero of brown as the stop rule when opportunity cost is ignored.

$$
c = 45
$$

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

With a constant opportunity cost of $6$, an extra cup is worthwhile only while $\mathrm{MU}-6>0$, i.e. while green is positive. The stop rule is green crossing zero:

$$
\mathrm{MU} = 6
$$

Do not stop where brown itself is largest or where brown hits zero; with opportunity cost present, the relevant crossing is green $=0$.

Green crosses zero near $c=30$ on the figure. Among the plotted options that is the best cup count — not the later zero of brown near $45$, which ignores the opportunity cost.

$$
c = 30
$$

which matches the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Falsch

Read the heights at $c=10$ carefully. Brown (marginal utility) sits at height $14$ there, and green is the parallel shift $\mathrm{MU}-6$.

$$
14-6 = 8
$$

If one mistakenly read brown's height $14$ as green's height, the claim would look true — subtracting the constant $6$ is the step that falsifies it.

Height $8$ lies below $10$, not above it. The trap is misreading brown's height as green's, or forgetting to subtract the constant $6$.

$$
c = 10
$$

which does not match the claim.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**D.** → Wahr

Utility $U$ has derivative $\mathrm{MU}$ (brown). A linear falling brown curve means $U^{\prime}$ has constant negative slope, so the second derivative is a negative constant:

$$
U^{\prime\prime} = (\mathrm{MU})^{\prime}<0
$$

Linear falling MU is the strongest form of diminishing marginal utility on this window: the second derivative never approaches zero. throughout the plotted range. Strict negativity of $U^{\prime\prime}$ is exactly strict concavity of $U$ on this range.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**E.** → Falsch

Grün ist eine parallele Abwärtsverschiebung von Braun um die Konstante $6$. Die optimale Becherzahl löst grün $=0$, d.h. $\mathrm{MU}=6$ - eine Gleichheit von Grenznutzen mit Opportun dazu.

Brown selbst ist lineare s, die auf das gesamte Fenster fallen, so dasssprachen keine inneren Details. Die Stop-Regel ist die Null von Grün, nicht eine Spitze von Braun; die Rollen der beiden Kurven zu verwechseln ist die Falle.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

MATH 11.190.title: Cold-Chain: Sportage-Index: Lieferstunden
MATH 11.190.context: A cold-chain delivery records a spoilage index $S(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2}+9t$ over $0\le t\le4$ hours after loading. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
MATH 11.190.solution_overview:
Spoilage over $0\le t\le 4$ is

$$S(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2}+9t$$

Differentiating and factoring,

$$
S^{\prime}(t) = 3t^{2}-12t+9 = 3(t-1)(t-3)
$$

$$S^{\prime\prime}(t)=6t-12$$

Sign chart of $S^{\prime}$: positive on $(0,1)$, negative on $(1,3)$, positive on $(3,4)$. So $t=1$ is a local maximum and $t=3$ is a local minimum, matching $S^{\prime\prime}(1)=-6<0$ and $S^{\prime\prime}(3)=6>0$.

Closed-interval levels: $S(0)=0$, $S(1)=4$, $S(3)=0$, $S(4)=4$. Both $t=1$ and $t=4$ attain the global maximum height $4$ on $[0,4]$, so that maximum is not unique to $t=1$.
statements: Spoilage has a local maximum at $t=1$.
Spoilage has a local minimum at $t=3$.
Among the critical points in $(0,4)$, the global maximum of $S$ on $[0,4]$ is at $t=1$.
$S^{\prime\prime}(1)<0$ and $S^{\prime\prime}(3)>0$, matching the local max / local min reading.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Verfeinerung der Verschwörungs-Zyklus durch die Verschwörungs-Zyklus, die durch die Versschneiden, die durch die Verschswerteszeiten des Zss. $$
S^{\prime}(t) = 3t^{2}-12t+9
$$ $$
S^{\prime}(t) = 3(t^{2}-4t+3) = 3(t-1)(t-3)
$$ Die Wurzeln $t=1$ und $t=3$ dieser Faktorisierung sind die einzigen inneren Kandidaten für lokale Verderbsextreme auf $(0,4)$.

Die beanspruchte Faktorisierung stimmt genau und die Ursachen $t=1$ und $t=3$ werden die spätere lokal-extreme Lektüren führen. Dieverthas-E-E Kommentar und dies –e!

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

Classify $t=1$ by the sign chart of $S^{\prime}=3(t-1)(t-3)$.

For $t\in(0,1)$ both factors are negative, so the product is positive and $S^{\prime}>0$. Between $1$ and $3$ the factor $(t-1)$ is positive while $(t-3)$ is negative, so $S^{\prime}<0$.

Equivalently,

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(1) = 6\cdot 1-12
$$

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(1) = -6<0
$$

 confirms the same local-max reading by the second-derivative test.

A $+$ to $-$ change at $t=1$ is a local maximum of spoilage.

$$
t = 1
$$

$$
S^{\prime} = 3(t-1)(t-3)
$$

which matches the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Wahr

Continue the same sign chart past $t=3$.

On $(1,3)$ one has $S^{\prime}<0$, and for $t>3$ both factors $(t-1)$ and $(t-3)$ are positive, so $S^{\prime}>0$.

Equivalently,

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(3) = 6\cdot 3-12
$$

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(3) = 6>0
$$

 confirms the same local-min reading by the second-derivative test.

A $-$ to $+$ change at $t=3$ is a local minimum of spoilage — spoilage falls into a trough there before rising again toward the right endpoint.

$$
t = 3
$$

which matches the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**D.** → Falsch

A local maximum among critical points need not be the unique global maximum on a closed interval. Compare levels at the endpoints and at every critical point.

$$
S(0) = 0
$$

$$
S(1) = 1-6+9 = 4
$$

$$
S(3) = 27-54+27 = 0
$$

$$
S(4) = 64-96+36 = 4
$$

On a closed interval the global maximum can sit at an endpoint even when an interior local max exists; here the endpoint $t=4$ ties the local peak.

Both $t=1$ and $t=4$ attain height $4$, so the global maximum on $[0,4]$ is not uniquely at $t=1$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**E.** → Wahr

The second-derivative test should match the local max / local min reading already obtained from the sign chart.

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(t) = 6t-12
$$

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(1) = 6-12
$$

$$
6 - 12 = -6
$$

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(1) = -6 = -6<0
$$

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(3) = 18-12
$$

$$
18 - 12 = 6
$$

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(3) = 6 = 6>0
$$

The second-derivative test and the first-derivative sign chart are two readings of the same geometry; agreement between them is what the claim records.

Negative second derivative at $t=1$ confirms a local max, and positive second derivative at $t=3$ confirms a local min — exactly the claimed match.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

MATH 11.191.title: Two workshops: compare P′ graphs and levels
MATH 11.191.context: Two neighbouring workshops $A$ (brown) and $B$ (green) plot marginal profit on one plane. Both start with $P_A(0)=P_B(0)=0$. Use the figure. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
MATH 11.191.solution_overview:
Workshops $A$ (brown) and $B$ (green) plot marginal profit $P_A^{\prime}$ and $P_B^{\prime}$, both starting from

$$
P_A(0) = P_B(0) = 0
$$

Brown crosses from positive to negative at $Q=6$, so $A$ has a local profit maximum there. At that same $Q=6$, green is still positive (zero only near $Q=9$), so $B$'s profit is still rising and $B$ would expand past $A$'s stationary output.

On $(0,6)$ brown lies above green, so $P_A^{\prime}>P_B^{\prime}$. Integrating from the common zero start yields $P_A(6)>P_B(6)$.

On $(6,9)$ brown is negative while green remains positive, so $A$ should contract and $B$ should expand. Where brown meets green (near $Q=3$), the shared height is a common marginal-profit value $P_A^{\prime}=P_B^{\prime}$, not the profit level $P_A(3)$.
statements: Workshop $A$ has a local profit maximum at $Q=6$.
Workshop $B$ still has positive marginal profit at $Q=6$, so $B$ would expand past $A$'s stationary output.
Because both start at profit $0$ and brown lies above green on $(0,6)$, it follows that $P_A(6)>P_B(6)$.
Auf $(6,9)$ sollte Workshop $A$ einen Vertrag abschließen, Workshop $B$ sollte erweitert werden.
The height where brown meets green (near $Q=3$) is the profit level $P_A(3)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Workshop $A$'s marginal profit is the brown curve. A local profit maximum occurs where brown crosses from positive to negative: that is where the first-order condition $P_A^{\prime}=0$ holds with a $+$ to $-$ sign change.

That crossing sits at $Q=6$ on the figure. Left of $6$, brown is positive so $A$'s profit is rising; right of $6$, brown is negative so profit is falling.

$$
P_A^{\prime} = 0
$$

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

Workshop $B$'s marginal profit is green. At $Q=6$, green still lies above the axis — it only reaches zero near $Q=9$.

Workshop $A$ has already hit $P_A^{\prime}=0$ at $Q=6$, while $B$ still has $P_B^{\prime}>0$ there — the two workshops' stationary outputs need not coincide.

Positive marginal profit means $B$'s total profit is still rising at the output where $A$ has already stopped. So $B$ would expand past $A$'s stationary output, which is exactly the comparison in the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Wahr

Both workshops start at profit zero. On $(0,6)$ brown lies above green, so $P_A^{\prime}>P_B^{\prime}$ throughout that interval. Integrating the strict inequality from the common start yields

$$
P_A(6)-P_A(0)>P_B(6)-P_B(0)
$$

and with $P_A(0)=P_B(0)=0$ one obtains $P_A(6)>P_B(6)$. The trap would be comparing heights of the $P^{\prime}$ curves at a single point instead of integrating the gap.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**D.** → Wahr

On $(6,9)$ brown lies below the axis while green still lies above it.

The interval $(6,9)$ is exactly the stretch where the two workshops' first-order advice diverges: $A$ wants less output, $B$ wants more.

Negative marginal profit tells workshop $A$ to contract (reduce $Q$); positive marginal profit tells workshop $B$ to expand (increase $Q$). Those are exactly the opposite directions named in the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**E.** → Falsch

Where brown meets green near $Q=3$, the two workshops share a common marginal-profit value:

$$
P_A^{\prime}(3) = P_B^{\prime}(3)
$$

Profit levels are areas under the $P^{\prime}$ curves from $0$; a single shared height of the derivative graphs does not equal either workshop's accumulated profit.

That shared height is a value of the derivatives, not a level of total profit. In particular it is not $P_A(3)$ — confusing the ordinate of a $P^{\prime}$ graph with a profit level is the trap.

$$
Q = 3
$$

which does not match the claim.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

MATH 11.192.title: Kiost-Kiosk: Nachfrage-Zahl plus quadratic Kosten
MATH 11.192.context: A print kiosk faces the demand curve $D(p)$ in the figure (quantity against price $p$). Production cost for $Q$ posters is $C(Q)=4Q+\dfrac{1}{20}Q^{2}$. Revenue is $R=p\cdot D(p)$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
MATH 11.192.solution_overview:
The figure's demand line is $D(p)=60-2p$, and production cost is

$$C(Q)=4Q+\dfrac{1}{20}Q^{2}$$

$$C^{\prime}(Q)=4+\dfrac{Q}{10}$$

$$
AC(Q) = 4+\dfrac{Q}{20},\qquad AC^{\prime}(Q) = \dfrac{1}{20}>0
$$

so average cost rises for every $Q>0$. Revenue $R(p)=p(60-2p)$ has $R^{\prime}(p)=60-4p$. At $p=15$, demand is $D(15)=30$, so $R=450$, and elasticity is $\varepsilon=\dfrac{-2p}{60-2p}=-1$.

Unit elasticity maximises revenue ($MR=0$), but at $Q=30$ one has $C^{\prime}(30)=7\neq 0$, so $p=15$ is not a profit maximum. At $p=10$, demand is $40$, $C^{\prime}(40)=8$, and $R^{\prime}(10)=20>0$.
statements: Reading the figure, $D(15)=30$, so revenue at $p=15$ equals $450$.
Price elasticity of demand at $p=15$ equals $-1$.
At $p=15$, marginal cost of the corresponding output equals $0$, so profit is maximised there.
At $p=10$, demand is $40$ and $MC=C^{\prime}(40)=8$, while a small price increase from $10$ still raises revenue.
Durchschnittliche Kosten $AC(Q)=\dfrac{C(Q)}{Q}$ steigt für jeden $Q>0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Revenue is price times quantity demanded. The figure marks the point $(15,30)$ on the demand curve, so

$$
D(15) = 30
$$

$$
R(15) = 15\cdot 30
$$

$$
15\times 30 = 450
$$

Equivalently, from the line $D=60-2p$ one computes

$$
D(15) = 60-30
$$

$$
60 - 30 = 30
$$

$$
D(15) = 30
$$

, then $R=pD=450$, matching the marked figure point.

That is the revenue at the named price — no elasticity or cost calculation is needed for this letter.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

Die Linie der Figur ist die lineare Nachfrage $D=60-2p$, mit Steigung $D^{\prime}=-2$. Point elasticity is $$
\varepsilon(p) = \dfrac{D^{\prime}(p)\,p}{D(p)} = \dfrac{-2p}{60-2p}
$$ At $p=15$, $$
\varepsilon = \dfrac{-2\cdot 15}{60-30} = \dfrac{-30}{30} = -1
$$ Für die lineare Nachfrage ist die Elastizität der Einheit auch der umsatzmaximierende Preis: $$
R^{\prime}(15) = 60-4\cdot 15
$$ $$
R^{\prime}(15) = 0
$$ Ich gen: Dass so gut.

Die Elastizität von Einheiten enthält zu diesem Preis an, wo auch die Einnahmen für die lineare Nachfrage Tischeseile haben.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Falsch

Die Elast der Einheit maximiert den Umsatz ( $MR=0$ ), nicht den Gewinn. At $p=15$ one has $Q=30$ und marginal cost is $$
C^{\prime}(Q) = 4+\dfrac{Q}{10}
$$ $$
C^{\prime}(30) = 4+3
$$ $$
4 + 3 = 7
$$ $$
C^{\prime}(30) = 7 = 7\neq 0
$$ Wegen des Versäumnisses, durch das der Fälligkeits-Fach geworfen wurde, sperrte sich der verwandelt Dass das am schlags- und fälligkeits-geschö- en des sens-sens-geschöpf, das durch das Fälls-fähiges------------------------------------------------------------------ des -------------------------------------.

Profit maximisation requires $MR=MC$. Hier $MR=0$ während $MC=7$, also $p=15$ ist eine Umsatzspitze, aber kein Gewinnmaximum - das ist die klassische Falle.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**D.** → Wahr

Read demand at $p=10$ from the figure, then evaluate marginal cost and the revenue derivative.

$$
D(10) = 60-20
$$

$$
60 - 20 = 40
$$

$$
D(10) = 40
$$

$$
C^{\prime}(40) = 4+\dfrac{40}{10} = 8
$$

All three pieces of the claim — demand $40$, $MC=8$, and $R^{\prime}(10)>0$ — are verified by direct substitution into the figure line and the cost rule.

With $R(p)=60p-2p^{2}$, one has $R^{\prime}(p)=60-4p$, so $R^{\prime}(10)=20>0$: a small price increase from $10$ still raises revenue.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**E.** → Wahr

Form average cost by dividing total cost by output, then differentiate.

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{C(Q)}{Q} = 4+\dfrac{Q}{20}
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(Q) = \dfrac{1}{20}>0
$$

Unlike a U-shaped average-cost curve with a positive fixed-cost term, this cost rule has no fixed cost, so $AC$ starts at $4$ and drifts upward linearly.

The derivative is a positive constant, so average cost is strictly increasing for every $Q>0$ — there is no U-shaped dip for this quadratic cost.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

MATH 11.193.title: Gewürz-Importeur: pro Einheit Steuersenken
MATH 11.193.context: A spice importer's MR (brown) and MC (green) are shown, together with post-tax marginal cost (purple) after a specific tax of $4$ per unit. Pre-tax they meet near $Q=16$; post-tax purple meets brown nearer $Q=\dfrac{40}{3}$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
MATH 11.193.solution_overview:
The figure shows pre-tax MR (brown) and MC (green), together with post-tax marginal cost (purple) after a specific tax of $4$ per unit — a parallel upward shift of green by $4$.

Pre-tax, brown meets green near $Q=16$. At $Q=12$ brown still lies above green, so expanding a little raises pre-tax profit. At $Q=20$, past that crossing, green already exceeds brown, so output is past the pre-tax optimum.

Post-tax, purple meets brown nearer $Q=\dfrac{40}{3}<16$. The new first-order condition is $MR=\mathrm{MC}+\mathrm{tax}$, so the tax lowers optimal output rather than raising it. Keeping the untaxed condition $MR=\mathrm{MC}$ with the old green curve would be wrong — the firm must use purple.
statements: Vorsteuer, die ein wenig von $Q=12$ ausdehnt, erhöht den Gewinn, weil Braun dort über grün ist.
Durch die Steuer wird die gewinnmaximierende Produktion angehoben.
Nach der Steuer, an der neuen Kreuzung der Firma gleicht MR zu MC plus die Steuer.
At $Q=20$, even pre-tax, green already exceeds brown, so that output is past the pre-tax optimum.
Because purple is a parallel upward shift of green by $4$, every post-tax optimum output must satisfy $MR=MC$ with the old green curve.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Profit rises while marginal revenue lies above marginal cost, and falls once MC overtakes MR. On the figure, at $Q=12$ brown (MR) still sits above green (MC), left of their pre-tax crossing near $Q=16$.

The pre-tax optimum is the later green–brown crossing near $Q=16$; at $Q=12$ one is still in the region where expanding raises profit.

Expanding a little from that output therefore adds more to revenue than to cost, raising pre-tax profit.

$$
Q = 12
$$

$$
Q = 16
$$

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Falsch

A specific tax of $4$ shifts marginal cost upward to the purple curve. The new $MR=\mathrm{MC}+\mathrm{tax}$ crossing is the purple–brown meeting near $Q=\dfrac{40}{3}$.

A higher per-unit cost schedule intersects the unchanged MR curve farther left, so optimal output contracts — the standard comparative-static of a specific tax.

That abscissa lies left of the pre-tax green–brown crossing near $Q=16$, so the tax lowers optimal output rather than raising it. The trap is thinking a cost shock expands production.

$$
Q = 16
$$

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**C.** → Wahr

Purple is the post-tax marginal cost — the old MC plus the tax of $4$ per unit. Where purple meets brown, the firm equates marginal revenue to that shifted cost schedule:

$$
MR = \mathrm{MC}+\mathrm{tax}
$$

In symbols, if green is $MC(Q)$ then purple is $MC(Q)+4$, and the post-tax stationary point solves $MR(Q)=MC(Q)+4$.

That is precisely the post-tax first-order condition, not a coincidence of the drawing.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**D.** → Wahr

The pre-tax optimum is the green–brown crossing near $Q=16$. At $Q=20$, which lies to the right of that crossing, green already exceeds brown: $MC>MR$.

Put differently: past the pre-tax FOC, the firm is on the wrong side of $MR=MC$, so cutting output toward $16$ would raise pre-tax profit.

Marginal cost above marginal revenue means each extra unit loses money, so that output is past the pre-tax optimum.

$$
Q = 16
$$

$$
Q = 20
$$

$$
MR = MC
$$

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**E.** → Falsch

Lila ist eine parallele Aufwärtsverschiebung von Grün um $4$, so dass die post-Steuer erster Ordnung Zustand verwendet lila, nicht die alte grüne Kurve.

Die parallele Verschiebung verändert das Interception für anderer noch dazu die Interception von MC, aber nicht deren Steigung; was für die FOC von Bedeutung ist, ist, dass die Firma nach die der Steuer folgt, nicht grün, sondern purple.

Entsprechend ist die Firma $MR=\mathrm{MC}+4$, nicht $MR=\mathrm{MC}$. Unterstützt dies mit den Traps, um dies zu verhindern. $$
MR = \mathrm{MC}+4
$$ $$
MR = \mathrm{MC}
$$ Die Aussage ist falsch.

MATH 11.194.title: Wie
MATH 11.194.context: Ein Marktgärtner zäunet ein dreiseitiges Kräuterbett mit $2x+y=60$ Meter Zaun (Fluss auf einer Seite) und verkauft die Ernte unter umgekehrter Nachfrage $p=24-\dfrac{1}{2}A$, wo $A=xy$ bepflanzt ist. Revenue is $R=pA$. Behandeln Sie $A$ als Mengenindex. Welche der folgenden Aussagen sind korrekt?
MATH 11.194.solution_overview:
Three-sided fencing $2x+y=60$ gives $y=60-2x$ and planted area

$$
A(x) = x(60-2x) = 60x-2x^{2}\qquad(0<x<30)
$$

$$
A^{\prime}(x) = 60-4x = 0\implies x = 15
$$

$$A^{\prime\prime}=-4<0$$

so area alone peaks at $x=15$ with $A(15)=450$. Under inverse demand $p=24-\dfrac{1}{2}A$, revenue as a function of area is

$$R(A)=24A-\dfrac{1}{2}A^{2}$$

$$
R^{\prime}(A) = 24-A = 0\implies A = 24
$$

far below $450$, so the area-maximising layout does not maximise revenue. Inverting demand, $A=48-2p$; at $A=24$ one has $p=12$ and $\varepsilon=\dfrac{-2p}{48-2p}=-1$.
statements: Eliminating $y$ gives planted area $A(x)=60x-2x^{2}$ for $0<x<30$.
Area alone (ignoring price response) is maximised at $x=15$.
Revenue $R(A)=24A-\dfrac12 A^{2}$ is maximised at $A=24$.
Das flächen- und flächenoptimierende darstellung läßt deine Einnahmen, weil $A=15\cdot30=450$ $24$ überschreitet.
Im ertragsmaximierenden Bereich $A=24$ entspricht die Preiselastizität der Nachfrage $-1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Eliminate the parallel side from the fencing budget and write planted area in the free length $x$.

$$
y = 60-2x
$$

$$
A(x) = x\cdot y = x(60-2x) = 60x-2x^{2}
$$

The factor $2$ in $2x$ comes from the two equal sides perpendicular to the river; the river itself supplies the fourth side for free.

The open fencing interval requires $y>0$ and $x>0$, so $0<x<30$, exactly as claimed. Matching the reduced area rule to the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → True

Maximise the concave quadratic area on that open interval, ignoring price response for this letter.

$$
A^{\prime}(x) = 60-4x = 0 \implies x = 15
$$

$$
A^{\prime\prime}(x) = -4<0
$$

At $x=15$ one has

$$
y = 60-30
$$

$$
60 - 30 = 30
$$

$$
y = 30
$$

 and planted area

$$
A = 15\cdot 30
$$

$$
15\times 30 = 450
$$

$$
A = 450
$$

, the largest rectangle the fence budget can enclose.

This letter maximises physical area alone; price response and revenue enter only in later letters.

So area alone is maximised at $x=15$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → Wahr

Revenue as a function of planted area is the quadratic coming from inverse demand $p=24-\dfrac{1}{2}A$.

$$
R(A) = pA = \left(24-\dfrac{1}{2}A\right)A = 24A-\dfrac{1}{2}A^{2}
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(A) = 24-A = 0 \implies A = 24
$$

This is a pure revenue calculation treating $A$ as the quantity index; the fencing constraint is set aside until one asks whether $A=24$ is feasible (it is).

And $R^{\prime\prime}=-1<0$, so revenue peaks at $A=24$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**D.** → Falsch

The area-maximising layout gives a huge planted area:

$$
A(15) = 60\cdot 15-2\cdot 15^{2} = 900-450 = 450
$$

Feasibility is not the issue — $A=450$ is attainable — but revenue at $A=450$ is dragged down by the low price

$$
p = 24-\frac12\cdot 450
$$

$$
p = -201
$$

, which is economically absurd on this demand line.

Revenue, however, peaks at $A=24$, far below $450$. Flooding the market with area drives price down along the inverse-demand line; maximising physical area is not the same as maximising revenue.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**E.** → True

Invert the demand rule to express quantity in terms of price, then evaluate elasticity at the revenue-maximising area.

$$
p = 24-\dfrac{1}{2}A
$$

$$
A = 48-2p
$$

At $A=24$ one has $p=12$, so

$$
\varepsilon = \dfrac{-2p}{48-2p} = \dfrac{-2\cdot 12}{48-24} = \dfrac{-24}{24} = -1
$$

For linear inverse demand, unit elasticity always marks the revenue peak:

$$
R^{\prime}(A) = 24-A = 0
$$

 at the same $A=24$ where $\varepsilon=-1$.

Unit elasticity at the revenue peak is exactly what the claim asserts.

So the statement is True.

MATH 11.195.title: APP-Aver:-
MATH 11.195.context: An app studio's cost is $C(Q)=80\sqrt{Q}$ for $Q>0$. The figure shows $AC$ (brown) and $MC$ (green). Which of the following statements is/are correct?
MATH 11.195.solution_overview:
App-St erhebt an. $C(Q)=80\sqrt{Q}$ $Q>0$, bildet sich abheben, mit $$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{80}{\sqrt{Q}}\quad(\text{brown}),\qquad MC(Q) = \dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}\quad(\text{green})
$$ so $MC=\dfrac{1}{2}AC$ at every $Q>0$. At $Q=16$, $$
AC(16) = 20,\qquad MC(16) = 10
$$ Anpassung der markierten Höhen. Die Grenzkosten bleiben positiv, $C^{\prime}(Q)=\dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}>0$, die Gesamtkosten steigen also streng an, selbst wenn so in beiden AC und MC fallen. Scaling gives $\dfrac{C(18)}{C(9)}=\sqrt{2}$ und $AC^{\prime}(Q)=-40Q^{-\frac{3}{2}}<0$, so a small increase in $Q$ near $Q=25$ still lowers average cost.
statements: At $Q=16$, the figure's brown height is $20$ and green height is $10$, matching $AC=\dfrac{80}{\sqrt{Q}}$ and $MC=\dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}$.
$MC=\dfrac12 AC$ at every $Q>0$ shown.
Because both curves fall, total cost $C(Q)$ is decreasing.
Doubling cumulative output from $9$ to $18$ multiplies total cost by $\sqrt{2}$.
A small increase in $Q$ near $Q=25$ lowers average cost.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Bewerten Sie die geschlossenen Formen bei $Q=16$ und vergleiche mit den markierten Höhen auf der Figur. $$
\sqrt{16} = 4
$$ $$
AC(16) = \dfrac{80}{4} = 20
$$ $$
MC(16) = \dfrac{40}{4} = 10
$$ Die Figur ist daher keine unabhängige Quelle von Zahlen; es ist der Graph dieser beiden geschlossenen Formen, an eine bequeme Abszachse.

Braun in der Höhe $20$ und grün in der Höhe $10$ stimmen genau mit diesen Formeln überein - die Figur und die Algere stimmen überein.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

For square-root total cost the two curves are proportional for every $Q>0$:

$$
AC = \dfrac{80}{\sqrt{Q}}
$$

$$
MC = \dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}
$$

$$
\dfrac{MC}{AC} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

Because both schedules are proportional to $Q^{-1/2}$, their ratio is the constant $\frac12$ everywhere — a hallmark of square-root total cost.

So $MC=\dfrac{1}{2}AC$ holds throughout the figure, not only at a special output.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Falsch

Falling average and marginal cost do not make total cost fall. Marginal cost is still positive:

$$
C^{\prime}(Q) = MC(Q) = \dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}>0
$$

Learning can make each extra unit cheaper than the last (falling MC) while the running total $C(Q)$ still climbs; watch the sign of $C^{\prime}$, not of $AC^{\prime}$. For every $Q>0$, so $C$ itself is strictly increasing. The claim confuses falling per-unit schedules with a falling total — a classic learning-curve trap.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**D.** → Wahr

The ratio of total costs at doubled cumulative output is the square-root scale factor.

$$
\dfrac{C(18)}{C(9)} = \dfrac{80\sqrt{18}}{80\sqrt{9}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{18}}{3} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{3} = \sqrt{2}
$$

Under this technology, cost is homogeneous of degree $\tfrac12$ in cumulative output, so a twofold scale-up of $Q$ multiplies $C$ by $2^{1/2}$.

Doubling output from $9$ to $18$ multiplies total cost by $\sqrt{2}$, not by $2$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**E.** → Wahr

Differentiate average cost and read the sign near $Q=25$.

$$
AC(Q) = 80Q^{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(Q) = -40Q^{-\frac{3}{2}}<0
$$

Even far out the learning curve, $AC^{\prime}$ stays negative (though small); there is no flat stretch where a tiny increase in $Q$ would leave $AC$ unchanged. For every $Q>0$, including $Q=25$. A small increase in output near twenty-five releases therefore still lowers average cost — the learning curve has not flattened to zero slope.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

MATH 11.196.title: Pop-up Galerie: Newton Quotient, Steuer und Elastizität Stub
MATH 11.196.context: A pop-up gallery's profit (hundreds of euros) is $P(x)=x^{2}-8x+25$ before a flat licence fee. Staffed hours are $x>0$. After the fee, profit is $P(x)-6$. Separately, ticket demand at price $p$ is $D(p)=40-p$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
MATH 11.196.solution_overview:
Pre-fee gallery profit is

$$P(x)=x^{2}-8x+25\qquad(x>0)$$

The Newton quotient simplifies to $\dfrac{P(a+h)-P(a)}{h}=2a+h-8$, so

$$
P^{\prime}(x) = 2x-8 = 2(x-4)
$$

with a $-$ to $+$ sign change at $x=4$: a local minimum. A flat licence fee subtracts the constant $6$, which vanishes upon differentiation, so $\dfrac{d}{dx}(P(x)-6)=P^{\prime}(x)$ and the same minimum remains with or without the fee. At $x=5$, $P^{\prime}(5)=2$.

Separately, ticket revenue $R(p)=p(40-p)$ has $R^{\prime}(p)=40-2p=0\implies p=20$, and at that price $\varepsilon=\dfrac{-p}{40-p}=-1$.
statements: The Newton quotient $\dfrac{P(a+h)-P(a)}{h}$ simplifies to $2a+h-8$.
The licence fee changes $P^{\prime}(x)$ at every $x$.
$x=4$ ist ein lokales Minimum an Galeriegewinn, Gebühr oder keine Gebühr.
Ticket revenue $R(p)=p(40-p)$ is maximised at $p=20$, where demand elasticity equals $-1$.
At $x=5$, pre-fee marginal profit equals $2$, so staffing one more hour raises profit by about $2$ hundred euros.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Erweitern Sie den verschobenen Gewinn, annullieren Sie $P(a)$ und teilen Sie durch das Inkrement $h$. $$
P(a+h) = (a+h)^{2}-8(a+h)+25 = a^{2}+2ah+h^{2}-8a-8h+25
$$ $$
P(a+h)-P(a) = 2ah+h^{2}-8h
$$ $$
\dfrac{P(a+h)-P(a)}{h} = 2a+h-8
$$ Versenden $h\to 0$ $P^{\prime}(a)=2a-8$ $P^{\prime}(a)=2a-8$, aber die Integral-Differenz-Vereinfachung, die immer noch den $+h$ Begriff trägt.

Der ⟘ suchen,, die sich in der Ableitung der, die in der Ableitung liegt.

Der Newton-Quotient vereinfacht sich auf $2a+h-8$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Falsch

Eine pauschale Lizenzgebühr subtrahiert die Konstante $6$ vom Gewinn. Constants vanish upon differentiation: $$
\dfrac{d}{dx}\bigl(P(x)-6\bigr) = P^{\prime}(x)
$$ Nur eine Gebühr, die von $x$ abhängig ist (eine variable Steuer oder eine stündliche Abgabe), würde $P^{\prime}$ ändern; eine Flachlizenz ist hoherre Verlagerung.

Die Gebühr ändert das Gewinnniveau (verschiebt den Graphen vertikal), aber lässt die Steigung $P^{\prime}$ bei jedem $x$ unberührt. Die Falle denkt, dass eine Pauschalgebühr den marginalen Gewinn kippt.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**C.** → Wahr

Locate the critical point of gallery profit from the first derivative.

$$
P^{\prime}(x) = 2x-8 = 2(x-4)
$$

Because $P^{\prime\prime}(x)=2>0$, the parabola opens upward, so the stationary point at $x=4$ can only be a minimum — fee or no fee.

At $x=4$ the derivative changes from negative to positive, so $x=4$ is a local minimum. Subtracting a constant fee does not alter $P^{\prime}$, so the same minimum remains with or without the fee.

$$
x = 4
$$

which matches the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**D.** → Wahr

Ticket revenue is the usual downward-opening parabola in price.

$$
R(p) = p(40-p) = 40p-p^{2}
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(p) = 40-2p = 0
$$

$$
p = 20
$$

At that price, demand is $D(20)=20$ and elasticity is

$$
\varepsilon = \dfrac{D^{\prime}p}{D} = \dfrac{-p}{40-p} = \dfrac{-20}{20} = -1
$$

For linear demand $D=40-p$, unit elasticity and the revenue FOC always coincide; here both pick out $p=20$.

Revenue peaks at unit elasticity.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**E.** → Wahr

Pre-fee marginal profit is simply $P^{\prime}$. Evaluate at five staffed hours:

$$
P^{\prime}(5) = 2\cdot 5-8 = 10-8 = 2
$$

That reading is the practical content of the derivative: a one-hour staffing increment near $x=5$ changes profit by about $P^{\prime}(5)$ hundred euros.

Staffing one more hour near $x=5$ therefore raises profit by about $2$ hundred euros — the Newton-quotient / derivative reading of a small increment.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

MATH 11.197.title: Gießerei: MC und MC′-Zahl für die Beugung der Gesamtkosten
MATH 11.197.context: Eine Gießerei zeichnet die Grenzkosten (braun) und die Ableitung der Grenzkosten (grün) auf. Total cost is $C$, so brown is $C^{\prime}$ und green is $C^{\prime\prime}$. Welche der folgenden Aussagen korrekt ist/s sind?
MATH 11.197.solution_overview:
The figure plots brown $=C^{\prime}$ (marginal cost) and green $=C^{\prime\prime}$ (the derivative of MC). By definition $C^{\prime\prime}=(C^{\prime})^{\prime}$, so an inflection of total cost is a zero of green with a sign change — equivalently a trough of brown.

Green crosses zero near $Q=4$, where brown has its minimum, so $C$ has an inflection there. On $(0,4)$ green is negative, so MC is decreasing and $C$ is concave down. At $Q=8$, green is positive and about height $4$, matching a rising MC.

Brown stays positive on the whole window, so $C^{\prime}>0$ and $C$ is strictly increasing throughout. A minimum of average cost is the different condition $MC=AC$; it need not coincide with the trough of brown where $C^{\prime\prime}=0$.
statements: Die Gesamtkosten haben eine Einbiegung in der Nähe von $Q=4$, wo grüne Kreuze Null und Braun ihr Minimum haben.
On $(0,4)$, green is negative, so marginal cost is decreasing und total cost is concave down.
Die durchschnittlichen Kosten sind auf ein Minimum genau in der Lage, dietwegen sie in der Lage sind, zu minimieren.
At $Q=8$, green is positive and about height $4$, matching a rising MC.
Da Braun am Fenster positiv bleibt, steigen die Gesamtkosten durchweg.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Brown is $C^{\prime}$ (marginal cost) und green is $C^{\prime\prime}$. Eine Umkehrung der Gesamtkosten ist eine Null von $C^{\prime\prime}$ mit einem Vorzeichenwechsel - äquivalent zu einem stationären Punkt von MC, an dem MC aufhört zu fallen und ansteigt.

Grüne Kreuze Null in der Nähe von $Q=4$ und das ist, wo Braun hat sein Minimum. Die Gesamtkosten haben also eine Knickung: Die Konkavität von $C$ dreht sich als MC-Boden heraus. $$
Q = 4
$$ Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

On $(0,4)$ green lies below the axis, so $C^{\prime\prime}<0$.

Past $Q=4$, green turns positive, so the same logic reverses: MC rises and $C$ becomes concave up.

Both readings — falling MC and concave-down $C$ — are the same second-derivative fact in two vocabularies.

Negative $C^{\prime\prime}$ means two things at once: marginal cost $C^{\prime}$ (brown) is decreasing, and total cost $C$ is concave down on that interval. Both readings follow from the same sign of green.

$$
Q = 4
$$

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Falsch

Average cost is minimised where $AC^{\prime}=0$, which rearranges (via the quotient rule) to the equality $MC=AC$.

One can have a falling-then-rising MC (an inflection of $C$) while $AC$ continues to fall until it later meets the rising MC from above.

A minimum of marginal cost alone — the trough of brown — is the different condition $C^{\prime\prime}=0$. Those two abscissae need not coincide; confusing a trough of MC with a trough of AC is the trap.

$$
AC^{\prime} = 0
$$

$$
MC = AC
$$

$$
C^{\prime\prime} = 0
$$

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**D.** → Wahr

At $Q=8$ the figure shows green positive and about height $4$.

In other words, green is the slope of brown; a positive green reading at $Q=8$ is precisely the statement that brown is climbing there.

Positive $C^{\prime\prime}$ means brown (marginal cost) has positive slope there — MC is rising. Height about $4$ is the rate at which MC is rising, matching the claimed reading of a rising MC.

$$
Q = 8
$$

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**E.** → Wahr

Brown is $C^{\prime}$. Wherever brown stays positive, total cost is strictly increasing: each extra unit still adds a positive amount to $C$.

An inflection or a trough of MC never by itself makes total cost fall — only a negative stretch of brown would do that, and none appears here.

On the plotted window brown never dips below the axis, so $C^{\prime}>0$ throughout and $C$ rises on the whole interval.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

MATH 11.198.title: Design duo: budget reduction then read U′ from the figure
MATH 11.198.context: A design duo has budget $2x+4y=40$ and output $U=xy$. After eliminating $y$ one obtains a single-variable $U(x)$ on $(0,20)$. The figure shows $U^{\prime}(x)$ for that reduced problem. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
MATH 11.198.solution_overview:
Budget $2x+4y=40$ and product $U=xy$ reduce, via $y=10-\dfrac{1}{2}x$, to the single-variable problem on $(0,20)$:

$$U(x)=10x-\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2}$$

$$U^{\prime}(x)=10-x$$

The figure plots that derivative: $U^{\prime}$ is positive on $(0,10)$, crosses zero from above at $x=10$, and is negative on $(10,20)$. So the reduced optimum is at $x=10$, where $y=10-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 10=5$, and $U^{\prime}(4)=6$ matches the marked height. Spending everything on $x$ forces $y=0$ at the right endpoint $x=20$, collapsing $U=0$ — the worst product value, not a maximum.
statements: Das reduzierte Optimum liegt bei $x=10$, wobei die Figur $U^{\prime}$ von oben Null kreuzt.
In diesem Optimum, $y=5$.
Auf $(0,10)$, $U^{\prime}>0$, so dass die Verschiebung eines kleinen Budgets vom Setzen in Richtung Illustration die Ausgabe erhöht.
The figure shows $U^{\prime}(4)=6$, matching $U(x)=10x-\dfrac12 x^{2}$.
Spending everything on $x$ ($y=0$) lands at the right endpoint where $U^{\prime}$ is most negative, hence maximises $U$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

After eliminating $y$ from the budget $2x+4y=40$, the reduced output $U(x)$ has derivative plotted in the figure. A maximum of reduced $U$ is a zero of $U^{\prime}$ with a $+$ to $-$ sign change.

Algebraically the same critical point solves

$$
U^{\prime}(x) = 10-x = 0 \implies x = 10
$$

, so $x=10$, matching the figure's zero crossing.

That crossing from above sits at $x=10$: left of $10$, $U^{\prime}>0$ so increasing $x$ raises $U$; right of $10$, $U^{\prime}<0$ so one should cut $x$.

which matches the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

Solve the budget for the complementary input and evaluate at the optimum $x=10$.

$$
4y = 40-2x
$$

$$
y = 10-\dfrac{1}{2}x
$$

$$
y = 10-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 10 = 10-5 = 5
$$

The pair $(x,y)=(10,5)$ spends the whole budget:

$$
2\cdot 10+4\cdot 5 = 20+20
$$

$$
20 + 20 = 40
$$

, so the optimum lies on the constraint as required.

Any other $y$ at $x=10$ would violate the budget; the constraint pins down the complementary input uniquely.

The matching typesetting intensity is $y=5$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Wahr

On $(0,10)$ the figure shows $U^{\prime}>0$. Increasing $x$ along the budget (and cutting $y$ accordingly) therefore raises the product $U=xy$.

Past $x=10$, $U^{\prime}$ turns negative, so the same logic would reverse: further shifts toward illustration would then lower output.

In the story, that is the same as shifting a little budget from typesetting toward illustration — moving right along the budget line while $U^{\prime}$ is still positive.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**D.** → Wahr

The reduced objective is the quadratic obtained by substituting $y=10-\dfrac{1}{2}x$ into $U=xy$.

$$
U(x) = x\left(10-\dfrac{1}{2}x\right) = 10x-\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2}
$$

$$
U^{\prime}(x) = 10-x
$$

$$
U^{\prime}(4) = 10-4
$$

$$
10 - 4 = 6
$$

$$
U^{\prime}(4) = 6
$$

The figure is therefore the graph of the linear derivative $10-x$; height $6$ at $x=4$ is a direct plug-in check, not an independent datum.

Height $6$ at $x=4$ matches the figure, confirming the reduced formula.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**E.** → Falsch

Spending everything on $x$ forces $y=0$ at the right endpoint $x=20$. The product utility then collapses:

$$
U = x\cdot 0 = 0
$$

A maximum of $U$ cannot occur where $U^{\prime}$ is most negative; that region is where one should move away from the endpoint, back toward $x=10$.

That corner is the worst product value, not a maximum. The negative $U^{\prime}$ near the endpoint merely says one should move left, back toward the interior mix $x=10$.

$$
y = 0
$$

which does not match the claim.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

MATH 11.199.title: Warehouse: EOQ mit Verderbsstrafe Overlay
MATH 11.199.context: Annual ordering-plus-holding cost is $TC(Q)=\dfrac{20000}{Q}+2Q$. Eine folgeweise ist ein verderbter Index entlang einer Lieferstunde $t\in[0,4]$ $S(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2}+9t$. Welche der folgenden Aussagen ist/sind korrekt?
MATH 11.199.solution_overview:
Annual inventory cost and the separate spoilage index are

$$TC(Q)=\dfrac{20000}{Q}+2Q$$

$$S(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2}+9t\qquad(t\in[0,4])$$

For the EOQ,

$$
TC^{\prime}(Q) = -\dfrac{20000}{Q^{2}}+2 = 0\implies Q = 100
$$

$$TC^{\prime\prime}(Q)=\dfrac{40000}{Q^{3}}>0\qquad(Q>0)$$

so $Q=100$ is a minimum. At that EOQ, with $h=4$, holding cost $\dfrac{hQ}{2}=2Q$ equals ordering cost $\dfrac{20000}{Q}$, both equal to $200$.

Separately, $S^{\prime}(t)=3(t-1)(t-3)$ gives a local max at $t=1$ and a local min at $t=3$, but $S(1)=S(4)=4$, so the global maximum on $[0,4]$ is not unique to $t=1$.
statements: The EOQ that minimises $TC$ is $Q=100$.
$TC^{\prime\prime}(Q)>0$ für alle $Q>0$, so dass der kritische Punkt ein Minimum ist.
$S^{\prime}(t)=3(t-1)(t-3)$, so spoilage has a local max at $t=1$ und a local min at $t=3$.
On $[0,4]$, the global maximum of $S$ is uniquely attained at $t=1$.
Beim EOQ sind die jährlichen Lagerkosten $\dfrac{hQ}{2}$ mit $h=4$ gleich den jährlichen Bestellkosten $\dfrac{KD}{Q}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Berechnen Sie die Ableitung von Gesamtinventar Kosten zu Null und lösen Sie für die wirtschaftliche Ordnung $$
TC^{\prime}(Q) = -\dfrac{20000}{Q^{2}}+2 = 0
$$ $$
Q^{2} = \dfrac{20000}{2} = 10000
$$ $$
Q = 100
$$ Dies ist das übliche EOQ-Gleichgewicht: die Ableitung von $KD/Q$ hebt die Ableitung von $hQ/2$ ab, wenn $Q=\sqrt{KD/(h/2)}=\sqrt{10000}$.

(die erntete kräftige Wurzel) Das ist die Frage, wie Sie die Frage mit der Frage, die Sie die Frage beantworten.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

Differentiate once more to classify the critical point.

$$
TC^{\prime\prime}(Q) = \dfrac{40000}{Q^{3}}
$$

Convexity of $TC$ on $(0,\infty)$ means there is only one critical point and it must be the global minimiser of annual inventory cost.

For every $Q>0$ this second derivative is strictly positive, so $TC$ is convex on the positive domain and the critical point $Q=100$ is a minimum.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Wahr

Differentiate the spoilage index and factor the quadratic.

$$
S^{\prime}(t) = 3t^{2}-12t+9 = 3(t^{2}-4t+3) = 3(t-1)(t-3)
$$

The spoilage overlay is independent of the EOQ calculation; it is a separate cubic on delivery hours, sharing only the chapter's differentiation toolkit.

The sign chart of that product gives a local maximum at $t=1$ ($+$ to $-$) and a local minimum at $t=3$ ($-$ to $+$), exactly as claimed.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**D.** → Falsch

Compare spoilage levels at the critical points and at the endpoints of $[0,4]$.

$$
S(1) = 1-6+9
$$

$$
1 - 6 = -5
$$

$$
-5 + 9 = 4
$$

$$
S(1) = 4
$$

$$
S(4) = 64-96+36 = 4
$$

On a closed interval the global maximum can sit at an endpoint even when an interior local max exists; here $t=4$ ties the local peak at height $4$.

Both abscissae attain the same height $4$, so the global maximum on the closed interval is not uniquely attained at $t=1$ — the right endpoint ties the local max.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**E.** → Wahr

At the EOQ the two cost pieces balance. With holding rate $h=4$, the annual holding cost is $\dfrac{hQ}{2}=2Q$, matching the rising term in $TC$.

$$
\dfrac{h\cdot 100}{2} = 2\cdot 100
$$

$$
2\times 100 = 200
$$

$$
\dfrac{20000}{100} = 200
$$

That balance is why the EOQ formula equates the two cost pieces: at the minimum of their sum, their derivatives cancel and their levels match under this linear-holding setup.

Ordering cost equals holding cost at $Q=100$ — the classic EOQ balance.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

MATH 11.200.title: Brauerei: Lesen Sie P ' und P, schließen Sie P ohne Zeichnung P
MATH 11.200.context: Eine Brauerei zeigt nur marginalen Gewinn $P^{\prime}$ (braun) und $P^{\prime\prime}$ (grün) - das Niveau $P$ wird weggelassen. Für die Zwecke des Artikels 4 gegensätzlich
MATH 11.200.solution_overview:
Only $P^{\prime}$ (brown) and $P^{\prime\prime}$ (green) are drawn. Turns of profit sit where brown crosses the axis with a sign change.

At $Q=2$ brown flips $-$ to $+$ (local minimum of $P$), and at $Q=8$ brown flips $+$ to $-$ (local maximum of $P$).

Green is the concavity meter: wherever green is negative, $P^{\prime\prime}<0$ and $P$ is concave down. On $(5,10)$ that holds. Near $Q=5$, brown peaks and green crosses zero — the steepest climb of profit, an inflection of $P$, not a maximum of the level.

On $(2,8)$ brown stays positive, so profit is strictly increasing despite the concavity flip at $Q=5$. Treating $P^{\prime\prime}=0$ as a profit maximum confuses an inflection with the true FOC $P^{\prime}=0$ at $Q=8$.
statements: Profit has a local minimum at $Q=2$ und a local maximum at $Q=8$.
Profit is concave down on $(5,10)$ because green is negative there.
The steepest climb of profit occurs near $Q=5$, where brown peaks and green crosses zero.
$Q=5$ s maximiert Profit, weil das ist, wo $P^{\prime\prime}=0$.
On $(2,8)$, brown is positive, so profit is increasing despite green changing sign at $5$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Brown is $P^{\prime}$. Local extrema of profit sit where brown crosses the axis and changes sign — you do not need the omitted level curve $P$ itself.

At $Q=2$, brown changes from negative to positive — a local minimum of $P$. At $Q=8$, brown changes from positive to negative — a local maximum of $P$.

Green is not needed for this letter: the first-derivative sign changes of brown alone classify the local min at $2$ and the local max at $8$.

Those are exactly the turns named in the claim.

$$
Q = 2
$$

$$
Q = 8
$$

which matches the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Wahr

Green is $P^{\prime\prime}$, the concavity meter for profit. Wherever green is negative, $P^{\prime\prime}<0$ and the profit level $P$ is concave down.

Concavity can change while profit is still rising or falling; green's sign is about bend, brown's sign is about ascent or descent.

On $(5,10)$ green lies below the axis, so profit is concave down there. Concavity is about the bend of $P$, not about whether $P$ is rising or falling.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Wahr

The steepest climb of profit is the peak of $P^{\prime}$ — the highest point of brown — where the slope of $P$ is largest.

Do not confuse this steepest-climb abscissa with a maximum of $P$: at $Q=5$ one has $P^{\prime}>0$, so profit is still increasing through the inflection.

That peak lines up with the zero of green ($P^{\prime\prime}=0$) near $Q=5$: an inflection of $P$ at which the climb is steepest.

$$
Q = 5
$$

which matches the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**D.** → Falsch

A zero of $P^{\prime\prime}$ marks an inflection of profit (a turn of the slope), not a maximum of the level $P$.

The true profit maximum is the later zero of brown at $Q=8$, where the slope of profit itself crosses from uphill to downhill.

Profit is maximised where $P^{\prime}=0$ with a $+$ to $-$ sign change, which occurs at $Q=8$, not at the inflection $Q=5$. Treating $P^{\prime\prime}=0$ as a profit maximum is the wrong first-order condition — a classic trap.

$$
Q = 5
$$

$$
P^{\prime\prime} = 0
$$

which does not match the claim.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**E.** → Wahr

Monotonicity of profit is governed by the sign of $P^{\prime}$ alone. On $(2,8)$ brown stays positive, so profit is strictly increasing on that interval.

In particular, between the local min at $2$ and the local max at $8$, profit climbs through the inflection at $5$ without turning back.

Green changing sign at $Q=5$ only flips concavity; an inflection inside an increasing stretch is entirely allowed — $P$ can bend while still climbing.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

Listenership $Q(a)=10a^{\frac{3}{4}}$ yields revenue $R(a)=8Q(a)$ and cost $C(a)=a+25$. Chain-rule marginal revenue of advertising is

$$Q^{\prime}(a)=\dfrac{15}{2}a^{-\frac{1}{4}}$$

$$R^{\prime}(a)=60\,a^{-\frac{1}{4}}$$

An interior profit maximum sets $R^{\prime}(a)=1$: $60\,a^{-\frac{1}{4}}=1\implies a=60^{4}$ (not $60^{2}$). At $a=16$, $R^{\prime}(16)=30>1$, so a little more advertising still raises profit. Since $Q^{\prime\prime}<0$, listenership is concave and $R^{\prime}$ is decreasing, but $R^{\prime}-1$ can still cross zero once — an interior profit max remains possible. Scaling fails to be linear: $\dfrac{Q(2a)}{Q(a)}=2^{\frac{3}{4}}\neq 2$.

At $a=16$, $R^{\prime}(16)=30>1$, so a little more advertising still raises profit.
Because $Q^{\prime\prime}(a)<0$, listenership is concave in $a$, but profit may still have an interior maximum.

R^{\prime}(a) = 8Q^{\prime}(a) = 8\cdot\dfrac{15}{2}a^{-\frac{1}{4}} = 60\,a^{-\frac{1}{4}}

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**B.** → Falsch

An interior profit maximum sets marginal revenue of advertising equal to the marginal cost of one more euro spent, which is $1$.

$$
60\,a^{-\frac{1}{4}} = 1
$$

$$
a^{\frac{1}{4}} = 60
$$

$$
a = 60^{4}
$$

Raising both sides to the fourth power is required because the exponent on $a$ in $R^{\prime}$ is $-1/4$; stopping at a square is an algebra slip.

The claim writes $a=60^{2}$, which understates the power — squaring instead of raising to the fourth.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**C.** → Wahr

Evaluate marginal revenue at the named spend and compare with marginal cost $1$.

$$

$$
a^{-\frac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

$$

$$

The profit derivative is $\pi^{\prime}(a)=R^{\prime}(a)-1$, so $R^{\prime}(16)-1=29>0$ confirms that profit is still rising at that spend.

So at $a=16$, an extra euro of advertising still adds more to revenue than to cost, and a little more advertising raises profit.

**D.** → Wahr

Concave listenership means $Q^{\prime\prime}<0$, so $R^{\prime}=8Q^{\prime}$ is strictly decreasing. The difference $R^{\prime}(a)-1$ can still cross from positive to negative exactly once.

That single sign change of $\pi^{\prime}$ is precisely an interior profit maximum. Concavity of $Q$ does not forbid an interior max of profit — it only makes $R^{\prime}$ downward-sloping.

$$

**E.** → Falsch

$$
\dfrac{Q(2a)}{Q(a)} = \dfrac{10(2a)^{\frac{3}{4}}}{10a^{\frac{3}{4}}} = 2^{\frac{3}{4}}\neq 2
$$

Diminishing returns to advertising are built into the exponent $\tfrac34<1$; linear scaling of listenership would require the exponent $1$.

MATH 11.202.title: schuu schuuen. en.

MATH 11.202.solution_overview:
The figure's inverse demand is the line $p=20-\dfrac{1}{2}Q$, so

$$R(Q)=20Q-\dfrac{1}{2}Q^{2}$$

$$MR=20-Q$$

Variable cost $C(Q)=4Q$ has $MC=4$. Profit maximisation (fee or no fee) solves $20-Q=4\implies Q=16$, and $p=20-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 16=12$.

The lump-sum membership fee $F=50$ shifts the profit level but vanishes in $\pi^{\prime}=MR-MC$, so it does not move optimal $Q$. At $Q=20$ one has $p=10$, so the variable margin is $pQ-C(Q)=200-80=120$ (not $150$). Inverting demand, $Q=40-2p$, and at $Q=20$ ($p=10$) one has $\varepsilon=\dfrac{-2p}{Q}=-1$.
statements: At $Q=20$, variable margin $pQ-C(Q)$ equals $150$.
Marginal revenue is $MR=20-Q$, so the quantity that maximises profit solves $20-Q=4$.
Der Mitgliedsbeitrag $F$ ändert die Gewinnmaximierung $Q$.
Bei diesem Optimum $Q=16$ ist der Preis $p=12$.
Preiselastizität bei $Q=20$ entspricht $-1$.

**A.** → Falsch

Read price at $Q=20$ from the inverse-demand figure and form the variable margin carefully.

At $Q=20$ one has

$$
p = 20-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 20
$$

$$
p = 10
$$

, so

$$
pQ-C(Q) = 10\cdot 20-4\cdot 20 = 200-80 = 120
$$

The membership fee $F$ is collected separately and does not enter the variable margin $pQ-C(Q)$; including it would be a different accounting object.

The claim asserts $150$, which overshoots the true margin $120$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**B.** → Wahr

The figure's inverse demand is the line $p=20-\dfrac{1}{2}Q$, so revenue and its derivative are

$$
R(Q) = \left(20-\dfrac{1}{2}Q\right)Q = 20Q-\dfrac{1}{2}Q^{2}
$$

$$
MR = R^{\prime}(Q) = 20-Q
$$

Profit maximisation sets $MR=MC=4$:

$$
20-Q = 4
$$

Solving that FOC gives

$$
Q = 16
$$

; the letter only needs the displayed equation $20-Q=4$, which already encodes $MR=MC$, which is exactly the claimed first-order condition.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Falsch

The membership fee $F=50$ is a lump-sum constant collected by the club. Differentiating with respect to $Q$ kills it:

$$
\pi(Q) = R(Q)-C(Q)+F
$$

$$
\pi^{\prime}(Q) = MR-MC
$$

Only a fee that varied with $Q$ (a per-member levy in the variable-cost schedule) would shift the $MR=MC$ crossing.

The fee shifts the profit level but leaves the $MR=MC$ condition — and therefore the optimal $Q$ — unchanged.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**D.** → Wahr

$$
20-Q = 4
$$

$$
Q = 16

p = 20-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 16 = 20-8 = 12

$$

$$
20 - 16 = 4
$$

$$
MR = 4
$$

$$
MR = MC
$$

, and inverse demand returns $p=12$, so both the FOC and the price reading hold.

Together, $Q=16$ and $p=12$ are the profit-maximising membership quantity and the price read from inverse demand.

At the optimum, price is $12$.

Invert demand to $Q=40-2p$ and evaluate point elasticity at $Q=20$ (where $p=10$).

$$
\varepsilon = \dfrac{-2p}{Q} = \dfrac{-2\cdot 10}{20} = -1
$$

For this linear demand, $MR=0$ at $Q=20$ as well ($20-Q=0$), so unit elasticity and the revenue peak again coincide.

So the elasticity claim is another reading of the same revenue-peak geometry already visible in $MR$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

MATH 11.203.title: Mill: average-cost drift and a rival's marginal revenue
MATH 11.203.context: A mill has cost $C(Q)=\dfrac13 Q^{3}-4Q^{2}+30Q+90$. Eine rivalisierende Mühle gleicht den Umsatz bei $Q=5$ aus, hat aber einen strikt größeren Grenzumsatz bei $5\le Q\le 8$. Welche der folgenden Aussagen ist/sind korrekt?
MATH 11.203.solution_overview:
Mill cost is

$$C(Q)=\dfrac{1}{3}Q^{3}-4Q^{2}+30Q+90$$

Average cost and its derivative are

$$AC(Q)=\dfrac{1}{3}Q^{2}-4Q+30+\dfrac{90}{Q}$$

$$AC^{\prime}(Q)=\dfrac{2}{3}Q-4-\dfrac{90}{Q^{2}}$$

(not the mishandled expression $Q-\dfrac{8}{3}-\dfrac{90}{Q^{2}}$). At $Q=6$, $AC^{\prime}(6)=-\dfrac{5}{2}<0$, so average cost is still falling. Critical points of $AC$ rearrange via the quotient rule to $MC=AC$. Differentiating total cost twice, $C^{\prime\prime}(Q)=2Q-8=0\implies Q=4$, an inflection of $C$. A rival matching revenue at $Q=5$ but with strictly larger MR on $[5,8]$ finishes with strictly larger revenue at $Q=8$ after integrating the gap.
statements: $AC^{\prime}(Q)=Q-\dfrac{8}{3}-\dfrac{90}{Q^{2}}$ nach dem Schreiben $AC=\dfrac{C}{Q}$.
At $Q=6$, average cost is still falling.
Der Umsatz des Konkurrenten bei $Q=8$ muss den Umsatz dieser Mühle bei $Q=8$ überschreiten.
Marginal cost equals average cost at every critical point of $AC$.
$C^{\prime\prime}(Q)=2Q-8$, so total cost has an inflection at $Q=4$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Falsch

Form average cost carefully before differentiating — divide each term by $Q$.

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{C(Q)}{Q} = \dfrac{1}{3}Q^{2}-4Q+30+\dfrac{90}{Q}
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(Q) = \dfrac{2}{3}Q-4-\dfrac{90}{Q^{2}}
$$

A quick numerical check: the claimed wrong derivative at $Q=6$ would be $6-\tfrac83-\tfrac{90}{36}=6-2.67-2.5\approx 0.83$, not the true $-2.5$.

The claim writes $Q-\dfrac{8}{3}-\dfrac{90}{Q^{2}}$, which mishandles the quadratic coefficient ($\tfrac{2}{3}$ becomes $1$) and the linear term ($-4$ becomes $-\tfrac{8}{3}$).

Die Aussage ist falsch.
**B.** → Wahr

Evaluate the correct derivative of average cost at $Q=6$.

$$
AC^{\prime}(6) = \dfrac{2}{3}\cdot 6-4-\dfrac{90}{36} = 4-4-\dfrac{5}{2} = -\dfrac{5}{2}<0
$$

Until $AC^{\prime}$ reaches zero, expanding output still lowers cost per unit even if total cost rises.

Negative $AC^{\prime}$ means average cost is still falling at output $6$ — the firm has not yet reached the bottom of the AC curve.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Wahr

The two mills match revenue at $Q=5$, and the rival has strictly larger marginal revenue on $[5,8]$. Integrating that strict inequality from the common start yields

$$
R_{\mathrm{rival}}(8)-R_{\mathrm{rival}}(5)>R(8)-R(5)
$$

Matching revenue at the left endpoint and then outpacing this mill's MR on the interval forces a strictly larger rival revenue at the right endpoint, and with $R_{\mathrm{rival}}(5)=R(5)$ one obtains $R_{\mathrm{rival}}(8)>R(8)$. The trap would be reversing the inequality direction.

$$
Q = 8
$$

$$
Q = 5
$$

$$
R_{\mathrm{rival}}(5) = R(5)
$$

which matches the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**D.** → Wahr

Critical points of average cost solve $AC^{\prime}=0$. Writing $AC=\dfrac{C}{Q}$ and applying the quotient rule rearranges that equation to

$$
AC^{\prime} = 0
$$

$$
\Longleftrightarrow
$$

$$
MC = AC
$$

Geometrically, $AC$ is falling while $MC<AC$ and rising while $MC>AC$; the crossing $MC=AC$ is exactly where $AC$ turns.

So at every critical point of $AC$, marginal cost equals average cost — a general identity, not special to this mill.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**E.** → Wahr

Differentiate total cost twice and locate the zero of the second derivative.

$$
C^{\prime}(Q) = Q^{2}-8Q+30
$$

$$
C^{\prime\prime}(Q) = 2Q-8 = 0 \implies 2Q = 8 \implies Q = 4
$$

On $(0,4)$ one has $C^{\prime\prime}<0$ (concave down) and on $(4,\infty)$ one has $C^{\prime\prime}>0$ (concave up), confirming the inflection.

The second derivative changes from negative to positive there, so $Q=4$ is an inflection of total cost.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

MATH 11.205.title: Destillerie: quadratische Kosten, lineare Nachfrage und Einheitssteuer
MATH 11.205.context: A distillery faces inverse demand $p=30-\dfrac13 Q$ and cost $C(Q)=\dfrac25 Q^{2}+8Q+60$. A unit tax of $5$ shifts the firm's marginal cost up by $5$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
MATH 11.205.solution_overview:
Inverse demand $p=30-\dfrac{1}{3}Q$ and cost $C(Q)=\dfrac{2}{5}Q^{2}+8Q+60$ give

$$R(Q)=30Q-\dfrac{1}{3}Q^{2}$$

$$MR=30-\dfrac{2}{3}Q$$

$$MC=\dfrac{4}{5}Q+8$$

Pretax $MR=MC$ solves $30-\dfrac{2}{3}Q=\dfrac{4}{5}Q+8\implies Q=15$. A unit tax of $5$ shifts MC to $\dfrac{4}{5}Q+13$, so the new FOC $MR=\dfrac{4}{5}Q+13$ yields a strictly smaller positive root than $15$.

Revenue peaks where $MR=0$: $Q=45$, with $p=15$ and $\varepsilon=-1$. The tax moves the profit FOC through MC but leaves the revenue schedule — and $MR=0$ — untouched.
statements: Pretax marginal revenue is $MR=30-\dfrac23 Q$.
Pretax profit is maximised at $Q=15$.
Nach der Steuer setzt die Firma $MR$ mit $\dfrac45 Q+13$ gleich, so dass der optimale Output strikt unter $15$ liegt.
Pretax revenue is maximised at $Q=45$, where price elasticity equals $-1$.
Es ibelt, daß die von.Μm- Slogans:.

**A.** → Wahr

Revenue is price times quantity under the given inverse demand. Expand and differentiate.

$$
R(Q) = \left(30-\dfrac{1}{3}Q\right)Q = 30Q-\dfrac{1}{3}Q^{2}
$$

$$
MR = R^{\prime}(Q) = 30-\dfrac{2}{3}Q
$$

In general, for inverse demand $p=a-bQ$ one has $MR=a-2bQ$; here $a=30$ and $b=\tfrac13$, so $MR=30-\tfrac23 Q$.

That is the pretax marginal revenue named in the claim — twice the slope of inverse demand, as always for linear demand. Matching the expression to the claim.

**B.** → Wahr

Pretax marginal cost comes from differentiating the quadratic cost rule.

$$

$$

Set $MR=MC$:

$$

22 = \dfrac{2}{3}Q+\dfrac{4}{5}Q = \dfrac{10}{15}Q+\dfrac{12}{15}Q = \dfrac{22}{15}Q
$$

$$
Q = 15
$$

The second-order check is immediate: $MR^{\prime}-MC^{\prime}=-\tfrac23-\tfrac45<0$, so the critical point is a maximum of pretax profit.

Pretax profit is maximised at $Q=15$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
**C.** → Wahr

A unit tax of $5$ shifts marginal cost up by $5$.

$$

$$

$$

, hence $Q=\tfrac{15\cdot 17}{22}<15$.

The new FOC is $MR=\dfrac{4}{5}Q+13$. Compared with the pretax equation that had $+8$ on the right, the same algebra now yields a strictly smaller positive root than $15$, so optimal output falls.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

$$

$$
Q = 45

$$

p = 15

. Inverting demand gives

Revenue maximisation ignores cost and tax alike; only the demand side enters $MR=0$.

**E.** → Falsch

Revenue depends only on the demand curve. A unit tax on the firm shifts marginal cost and therefore moves the profit-maximising output, but it leaves the revenue schedule — and the condition $MR=0$ — untouched.

$$
MR = 0
$$

$$
Q = 45
